Paper 2 Exam Guide: How to Answer Every Question

50 Minutes • 28 Marks
The Three Question Types • What the Examiner Wants Total Time: 50 Minutes
Q1: One Consequence (4 Marks • 6 Mins)
• Question: "Explain one consequence of [an event]..."
• What to write: Write ONE clear paragraph.
• Formula: State the consequence clearly in sentence 1. Then give 2 detailed facts. Finish by explaining what happened because of it.
• Important: Do NOT write an introduction, conclusion, or a second consequence! You only get marks for ONE.
Q2: Narrative Account (8 Marks • 14 Mins)
• Question: "Write a narrative account analysing..."
• What to write: Tell the historical story in 3 paragraphs: Beginning ➔ Turning Point ➔ Outcome.
• Formula: Link every paragraph using connecting words like As a result, Because of this, or This led to.
• Important: You get 2 bullet points on the exam paper. You MUST also include facts from your own knowledge!
Q3: Importance of Two (16 Marks • 24 Mins)
• Question: "Explain the importance of TWO of the following..."
• Choice: Choose strictly TWO out of three options (8 marks each). Never attempt all three!
• Structure: Write 2 paragraphs for each option you choose.
• Para 1: What was the immediate impact of the event?
• Para 2: What was the long-term impact on peace or conflict?
Four Golden Rules for Success
1. Use Specific Facts: Always include real names, dates, and numbers (e.g. UN Resolution 242, King David Hotel, 700,000 refugees).
2. Use Linking Words: In Question 2, show how one event caused the next (e.g. This directly caused, Consequently).
3. Explain the Impact: In Question 3, don't just describe the story; explain why it made a big difference to peace or war.
4. Watch the Clock: Spend exactly 6 minutes on Q1, 14 minutes on Q2, and 24 minutes on Q3. Stop at 50 minutes!
⭐ Model Answers (WAGOLL): Clear Examples of Top-Mark Answers See How to Structure Your Writing
Q1 Model: Consequence of the 1948 War [4 Marks]

"One consequence of the 1948–49 Arab-Israeli War was the creation of a massive Palestinian refugee crisis. During the fighting, over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were forced out of their homes in what became known as Al-Nakba. Israel refused to let them return after the war because it wanted to protect its Jewish majority. As a result, hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were forced to live in permanent refugee camps in Gaza, the West Bank, and Jordan, run by the UN agency UNRWA."

Why this scores 4/4: States the consequence in line 1 • Gives exact facts (700,000, Al-Nakba, UNRWA) • Explains the result clearly.
Q2 Model: Events Leading to the 1956 Suez Crisis [8 Marks]

"The crisis began in July 1956 when President Nasser of Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal after the USA cancelled loans to build the Aswan Dam. Because the canal was owned by Britain and France, both countries were furious and wanted to regain control. As a result, Britain and France held secret talks with Israel at Sèvres in October 1956, agreeing that Israel would invade Egypt so Britain and France could step in to 'protect' the canal. The turning point came when US President Eisenhower threatened to cut off financial loans to Britain. Consequently, Britain and France were forced into a humiliating retreat, leaving Nasser with the canal."

Why this scores 8/8: Tells the story in clear chronological order • Uses linking words in every step • Includes own knowledge (Aswan Dam, Sèvres).
⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid on Exam Day
• Don't write two consequences for Q1: Examiners only mark your FIRST consequence. Writing a second wastes time.
• Don't answer all three options in Q3: You only get marks for TWO. Answering all three wastes 12 minutes!
• Don't just write a list of events in Q2: Always explain why one event caused the next event to happen.

Key Chronology • The Complete 50-Year Story (1945–1995)

50-Year Timeline: From the Creation of Israel to the Oslo Accords

Master Timeline
Key Topic 1: Birth of Israel (1945–63)
July 1946: Irgun bombs British military HQ at King David Hotel (91 dead).
Feb 1947: Britain gives up Mandate and asks the UN to take over.
July 1947: Royal Navy intercepts SS Exodus with 4,500 refugees.
Nov 1947: UN passes Res 181 to divide Palestine (55% Jewish / 44% Arab).
9 Apr 1948: Deir Yassin massacre; Palestinian civilians flee in fear.
14 May 1948: David Ben-Gurion declares the independent State of Israel.
15 May 1948: Five Arab armies invade; First Arab-Israeli War starts.
1949: Armistice agreements set the Green Line; Israel holds 79% of land.
1949: Over 700,000 Palestinians become refugees in UNRWA camps (Al-Nakba).
1950: Israel passes Law of Return; population doubles in 3 years.
July 1956: President Nasser nationalises the Suez Canal.
Oct–Nov 1956: Suez Crisis; Israel invades Sinai; USA forces UK withdrawal.
Key Topic 2: Escalating Conflict (1964–73)
Jan 1964: Arab leaders meet in Cairo; PLO is formed; Water Wars begin.
Nov 1966: Israel launches major reprisal raid on Samu in the West Bank.
7 Apr 1967: Israeli jets shoot down 6 Syrian MiG planes over Damascus.
May 1967: Nasser expels UN troops, moves 100,000 soldiers, shuts Tiran Straits.
5–10 June 1967: Six-Day War; Israel captures Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, Golan.
Aug 1967: Arab summit at Khartoum declares 'Three Noes' (no peace, no recognition).
Nov 1967: UN passes Resolution 242 establishing 'Land for Peace' formula.
1969–70: War of Attrition; heavy artillery battles along the Suez Canal.
Sept 1970: Dawson's Field plane hijackings; Black September in Jordan.
Sept 1972: Black September terrorists kill 11 Israeli athletes at Munich Olympics.
6 Oct 1973: Yom Kippur War; surprise Egyptian & Syrian attack on holy day.
Oct 1973: Arab OPEC states launch oil embargo, quadrupling world oil prices.
Key Topic 3: Search for Peace (1974–95)
1974–75: Henry Kissinger uses 'shuttle diplomacy'; Suez Canal reopens.
Nov 1974: Yasser Arafat addresses UN General Assembly ('gun and olive branch').
19 Nov 1977: Anwar Sadat visits Jerusalem and speaks to the Israeli Knesset.
Sept 1978: President Carter brokers Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel.
26 Mar 1979: Treaty of Washington signs formal peace; Sinai returned to Egypt.
6 Oct 1981: Anwar Sadat is assassinated in Cairo by Islamic extremists.
June 1982: Israel invades Lebanon; Arafat and PLO are evacuated to Tunisia.
Sept 1982: Sabra and Shatila refugee camp massacres; Sharon forced to resign.
Dec 1987: First Palestinian Intifada begins in Gaza and West Bank (stone-throwing).
Nov 1988: Yasser Arafat renounces terrorism and accepts UN Resolution 242.
13 Sept 1993: Oslo I Accords signed at White House; Rabin and Arafat shake hands.
1994–95: Israel-Jordan peace treaty; Oslo II divides West Bank; Rabin assassinated.
Four Big Themes to Remember (1945–1995) Essential Ideas for Your Exam
1. The Superpowers (USA & USSR) The Cold War shaped the Middle East. The USA gave money and weapons to Israel. The Soviet Union armed Egypt and Syria. In 1973, US weapons saved Israel. When the USSR collapsed in 1991, the USA became the sole peace broker.
2. The Palestinian People In 1948, 700,000 Palestinians became refugees. In 1964, the PLO was formed to fight for their homeland. In the 1970s, militant groups turned to plane hijackings. In 1987, the First Intifada showed their determination, leading to the Oslo Accords.
3. The Arab-Israeli Wars Four major wars were fought: 1948 (survival), 1956 (Suez), 1967 (Six-Day War / territories captured), and 1973 (Yom Kippur). The 1973 war broke the myth of Israeli invincibility and proved that a military stalemate could only be solved by talks.
4. The Search for Peace Peace was achieved step-by-step: Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy (1974–75), Camp David and peace with Egypt (1979), peace with Jordan (1994), and the Oslo Accords (1993–95). However, extremist violence repeatedly threatened progress.
💡 Examiner Tip: The Big Picture Across 50 Years

Notice how the conflict changed: from 1948 to 1973, it was a war between countries (Israel vs Arab states). After 1973, Arab states began making peace (Egypt in 1979, Jordan in 1994), and the focus shifted directly to the Palestinians fighting for self-determination in the West Bank and Gaza.

Cartographic Atlas 1 • The 1947 Territorial Division

The 1947 United Nations Partition Plan (Resolution 181)

Map Atlas 1
1. The Land Split (55% vs 44%)
• Jewish State (55%): Given to ~500,000 Jews and ~400,000 Arabs. Included the fertile coastal plain and the large Negev desert.
• Arab State (44%): Given to ~725,000 Arabs and ~10,000 Jews. Included the hilly areas of Judea, Samaria, and Western Galilee.
• Population Difference: Arabs were two-thirds of the population, but were allocated less than half of the land.
2. Conflicting Reactions
• Jewish Leaders (Ben-Gurion): Accepted the plan because it gave international legal recognition to a Jewish state.
• Arab Leaders: Completely rejected the plan, arguing that Britain and the UN had no right to give away Arab land without consent.
• The UN Vote: Passed on 29 November 1947 with 33 votes in favour, 13 against, and 10 abstentions (including Britain).
3. The Problem with the Borders
• Divided into Pieces: Both states were broken into 3 separate pieces that only touched at tiny crossroads, making defence very difficult.
• Jerusalem: Placed under international control (run by the UN) so neither Jews nor Arabs owned the holy city.
• British Withdrawal: Britain refused to help carry out the plan, leaving in May 1948 without keeping order.
4. Immediate Result (Exam Link)
• Civil War Begins: Fighting between Arabs and Jews broke out the very next day (30 November 1947).
• Deir Yassin & Panic: In April 1948, Jewish fighters attacked the village of Deir Yassin, causing panic and mass civilian flight.
• Leads to 1948 War: When Britain left on 14 May 1948, Israel declared independence and five Arab armies invaded.
GCSE History Revision Guide • Option P5: Conflict in the Middle East Page 4 of 20 • 1947 UN Partition Plan Atlas
Cartographic Atlas 1 • The 1948–49 Arab-Israeli War

The 1948 Arab Invasions & The First Arab-Israeli War

Map Atlas 1
1. The Five Arab Invasions (15 May 1948)
• Egypt (11,000 soldiers): Advanced through Gaza along the coast towards Tel Aviv; halted 35km away by Israeli defences.
• Jordan (Arab Legion): Well-trained by British officers; captured the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank.
• Syria, Iraq & Lebanon: Attacked from the north and east; Syrian troops were stopped in heavy fighting around Galilee.
2. The Crucial June Truce
• Four-Week Ceasefire (11 June):** The UN arranged a temporary truce; both sides were banned from importing weapons.
• Czech Arms Import:** Israel secretly bought rifles, machine guns, and fighter planes from Czechoslovakia, giving it superior firepower.
• IDF Reorganisation:** Ben-Gurion united separate underground groups into one disciplined Israeli Defence Force (IDF).
3. The 1949 Green Line Borders
• Israel Expands:** Israel won the war and took **79% of the land** (far more than the 55% given by the UN plan).
• Jordan & Egypt:** Jordan kept the West Bank and East Jerusalem; Egypt kept the Gaza Strip.
• No Palestinian State:** Palestine was completely wiped off the map, divided between Israel, Jordan, and Egypt.
4. The Refugee Crisis (Al-Nakba)
• 700,000 Flee:** Over **700,000 Palestinian Arabs** lost their homes and land, fleeing to neighbouring Arab countries.
• UNRWA Camps:** Refugees lived in crowded tent camps, dependent on food rations from the United Nations.
• Ongoing Conflict:** Arab states refused to recognise Israel, and displaced Palestinians began cross-border fedayeen raids.

Lesson 1: Broken Promises & The British Mandate (1915–1945)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 1 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Conflicting British wartime promises (McMahon-Hussein & Balfour Declaration) • British Mandate and Jewish immigration • 1936–39 Arab Revolt • 1939 White Paper limits.
1. Conflicting British Promises
McMahon Letter & Balfour (1915–17)
  • McMahon-Hussein (1915): Britain promised Arab leaders independence if they rebelled against the Ottoman Empire during WW1.
  • Balfour Declaration (1917): Britain promised Jewish leaders support for a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine.
  • Sykes-Picot Agreement (1916): Britain and France secretly agreed to divide the Middle East between themselves after the war.
⚡ Why It Matters: Britain promised the same land to both Arabs and Jews during WW1, giving both sides legal claims.
2. The British Mandate & Rising Tension
Immigration & The Arab Revolt
  • League of Nations Mandate (1920): Britain was placed in charge of Palestine and tasked with preparing it for independence.
  • Rising Jewish Immigration: In the 1930s, thousands of Jewish people fled Nazi Germany to live in Palestine, alarming local Arabs.
  • 1936–39 Arab Revolt: Arab Palestinians rebelled against British rule and Jewish immigration; Britain crushed the revolt using military force.
⚡ Why It Matters: Rising Jewish immigration during the 1930s caused Arab fear of losing land, leading to violence.
3. The 1939 White Paper
Immigration Limits Anger Both Sides
  • Immigration Capped: Britain limited Jewish immigration to 15,000 people per year for 5 years (75,000 total).
  • Jewish Reaction: Jews were furious because the policy trapped millions in Europe just as the Holocaust was beginning.
  • Arab Reaction: Arabs were also unhappy because the White Paper did not grant them immediate independence.
⚡ Why It Matters: The 1939 White Paper limited immigration just as the Holocaust began, angering both sides.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: WW1 Promises
Britain made contradictory promises to both Arabs (1915) and Jews (1917) to win wartime support.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Jewish Immigration
Thousands of Jews fled Nazi persecution in the 1930s, causing fear and anger among local Arab communities.
3. KEY EVENT Clashes: 1936–39 Arab Revolt
Arabs launched a 3-year revolt against British rule; Britain crushed the rebellion with 20,000 soldiers.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: 1939 White Paper
Britain capped Jewish immigration at 15,000 a year, leaving both sides angry and ready to fight for the land.

Lesson 2: End of the British Mandate & Creation of Israel (1945–1949)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 2 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: End of the British Mandate • Jewish resistance (King David Hotel bombing) • UN Resolution 181 partition plan • Declaration of the State of Israel (14 May 1948) • The 1948–49 War.
1. Jewish Attacks on British Rule
King David Hotel & SS Exodus
  • Holocaust Survivors: 250,000 survivors were stuck in refugee camps in Europe; Britain refused to let them into Palestine.
  • King David Hotel (22 July 1946): Jewish group Irgun bombed British military HQ, killing 91 people; Britain lost control.
  • The SS Exodus (July 1947): Royal Navy sent a ship carrying 4,500 refugees back to Germany, causing worldwide outrage.
⚡ Why It Matters: Attacks by Jewish armed groups and the King David Hotel bombing proved Britain could no longer rule.
2. The UN Partition Plan (1947)
Resolution 181 Divides the Land
  • Britain Gives Up (Feb 1947): Britain announced it would leave Palestine and let the United Nations decide what to do.
  • UN Resolution 181 (Nov 1947): Proposed dividing Palestine: 55% for a Jewish state and 44% for an Arab state.
  • Arab Reaction: Arabs rejected the plan because they made up two-thirds of the population but got less than half the land.
⚡ Why It Matters: UN Resolution 181 gave international approval for a Jewish state, but Arabs rejected losing half their land.
3. Independence & The 1948 War
14 May 1948 & The Five Arab Armies
  • Israel Declared (14 May 1948): David Ben-Gurion announced the independent State of Israel as British troops pulled out.
  • Five Armies Invade (15 May 1948): Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon invaded Israel the very next day.
  • Why Israel Won: Israel had unified leadership (IDF), purchased weapons from Czechoslovakia, and fought with high motivation.
⚡ Why It Matters: David Ben-Gurion declaring Israel led immediately to five Arab armies invading the next day.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: King David Bombing
Irgun bombed British headquarters at the King David Hotel (July 1946), killing 91 people.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: UN Resolution 181
Britain handed Palestine to the UN; the UN voted in Nov 1947 to divide the land into Jewish and Arab states.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Declaration of Israel
On 14 May 1948, David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel as British soldiers left.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: 1948–49 War
Five Arab armies invaded the next day; Israel defeated them and expanded its territory to 79% of Palestine.

Lesson 3: Aftermath of the 1948–49 War & The Refugee Crisis

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 3 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Territorial changes and the 1949 Green Line • The Palestinian refugee crisis (Al-Nakba) • The Law of Return (1950) • Creation of the IDF • US financial aid to Israel.
1. The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
Al-Nakba ("The Catastrophe")
  • 700,000 Flee: Over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from their homes during the fighting.
  • UNRWA Refugee Camps: Most refugees lived in squalid tents in the West Bank, Gaza, Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon.
  • No Right of Return: Israel refused to let refugees return, fearing they would destroy the Jewish majority of the state.
⚡ Why It Matters: Over 700,000 Palestinians became permanent refugees in camps, creating an ongoing conflict.
2. New Borders: The Green Line
1949 Armistice Agreements
  • Israel Expands: Israel increased its control from 55% under the UN plan to 79% of historic Palestine.
  • Jordan & Egypt: Jordan took control of the West Bank and East Jerusalem; Egypt took control of the Gaza Strip.
  • No Peace Treaties: Arab nations signed ceasefires (armistices) but refused to sign permanent peace treaties or recognise Israel.
⚡ Why It Matters: The 1949 armistices created the Green Line borders, but Arab states refused to recognise Israel.
3. Building the State of Israel
Law of Return & The IDF
  • Law of Return (1950): Granted every Jewish person in the world the legal right to move to Israel and become a citizen.
  • Population Doubled: Israel welcomed 688,000 new Jewish immigrants by 1951, many fleeing Arab countries and Europe.
  • Creation of the IDF: Israel created a strong national army (IDF) with compulsory military service for all young citizens.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Law of Return allowed Jewish people worldwide to settle in Israel, doubling its population.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: 1948 War Displacement
During the 1948 war, over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Armistice Borders
1949 armistice talks created the Green Line; Israel controlled 79% of the land, but Arab states refused peace.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Law of Return (1950)
Israel passed the Law of Return (1950), bringing in 688,000 Jewish immigrants to build the new state.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Permanent Refugee Crisis
Palestinians remained trapped in UN refugee camps, leading to fedayeen border raids and ongoing conflict.

Lesson 4: Increased Tension, Nasser & The Suez Crisis (1955–1963)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 4 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: President Nasser and Pan-Arabism • 1955 Czech Arms Deal • Nationalisation of the Suez Canal (1956) • Secret Sèvres Agreement • Suez War and superpower intervention.
1. The Rise of Nasser
Pan-Arabism & The Czech Arms Deal
  • Leader of the Arabs: Nasser became President of Egypt in 1954, promising to unite Arab nations and stand up to the West.
  • Czech Arms Deal (1955): Nasser bought modern Soviet tanks and fighter jets from Czechoslovakia, alarming Israel and the West.
  • Fedayeen Raids: Nasser encouraged Palestinian fighters (fedayeen) to launch raids into Israel from the Egyptian-controlled Gaza Strip.
⚡ Why It Matters: Buying Soviet weapons from Czechoslovakia and taking the canal made Nasser the hero of the Arab world.
2. Canal Nationalisation & Sèvres Pact
Aswan Dam & The Secret Collusion
  • Canal Nationalised (July 1956): After the USA cancelled aid for the Aswan High Dam, Nasser seized the British/French-owned canal.
  • Secret Sèvres Pact (Oct 1956): Britain, France, and Israel held secret talks in France to plan a joint attack against Egypt.
  • The Plan: Israel would invade Egypt across Sinai; Britain and France would then pretend to step in as "peacekeepers" to seize the canal.
⚡ Why It Matters: The secret attack by Britain, France, and Israel failed when the USA threatened financial ruin.
3. The Suez War & The Results
US Intervention & British Humiliation
  • Invasion (29 Oct 1956): Israeli forces swept across Sinai in days; British and French paratroopers landed at Port Said.
  • US Economic Threat: US President Eisenhower was furious; he threatened to cut off financial loans to Britain unless they stopped.
  • The Outcome: Britain and France withdrew in disgrace; Nasser kept the canal; UN peacekeepers (UNEF) were placed on the border.
⚡ Why It Matters: The crisis showed Britain and France were no longer world powers; the USA and USSR took over.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Canal Nationalisation
Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956 to use its tolls to fund the Aswan High Dam.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Secret Sèvres Pact
Britain, France, and Israel met secretly at Sèvres to plan an attack to recapture the canal.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Invasion of Egypt
Israel invaded Sinai on 29 Oct 1956; British and French forces landed to seize the canal.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: US Halts the Attack
US President Eisenhower forced Britain and France to pull out, leaving Nasser as the undisputed hero of the Arab world.

Pan-Arabism The movement led by President Nasser to unite all Arab countries into one powerful community.
Sèvres Protocol The secret agreement made in October 1956 between Britain, France, and Israel to attack Egypt.
UNEF The United Nations Emergency Force sent to Sinai to act as a buffer between Egyptian and Israeli armies.
📜 KEY HISTORICAL EVIDENCE: Radio Broadcast to the Egyptian People in Alexandria
"The Suez Canal is Egyptian property... We shall build the High Dam on our own resources and with our own hands!"
💡 What This Shows: Demonstrates Nasser standing up to British and French colonial control, triggering the Suez Crisis.
👥 Key People
Gamal Abdel Nasser President of Egypt who nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956 and became the hero of Arab nationalism.
Anthony Eden British Prime Minister who colluded with France and Israel to attack Egypt, ending his political career in disgrace.

Lesson 5: Causes of the Six-Day War: Water, Raids & Rhetoric (1964–1967)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 5 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Causes of the Six-Day War • 1964 Cairo Conference & creation of the PLO • Water Wars & Fatah raids • Samu Raid (1966) & April 1967 dogfight • Closure of the Straits of Tiran.
1. The Water Wars & The PLO
Cairo Conference & National Water Carrier
  • Creation of the PLO (1964): Arab leaders created the Palestine Liberation Organisation to represent Palestinians and liberate Palestine.
  • Water Diversion Dispute: Arab states tried to divert the headwaters of the River Jordan; Israel bombed the diversion works to protect its water supply.
  • Fatah Border Raids: Palestinian guerrilla group Fatah, led by Yasser Arafat, carried out over 70 sabotage attacks inside Israel.
⚡ Why It Matters: Disputes over River Jordan water and guerrilla raids pushed Israel and Syria into open fighting.
2. Violent Border Clashes (1966–67)
The Samu Raid & The Syrian Dogfight
  • Samu Raid (Nov 1966): After an Israeli police car hit a landmine, Israeli forces attacked the West Bank town of Samu, damaging Jordan's relations with Israel.
  • April 1967 Dogfight: Israeli fighter jets shot down six Syrian MiG-21 planes and flew over Damascus, humiliating the Syrian government.
  • Rising Hatred: Arab radio stations broadcast aggressive speeches promising to drive Israel into the sea and destroy the Jewish state.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Samu Raid and the downing of 6 Syrian planes humiliated Arab leaders and increased pressure for war.
3. Nasser's May 1967 Escalation
UNEF Expelled & The Straits Blockaded
  • False Soviet Warning: The USSR falsely told Egypt that Israel was massing troops to invade Syria, pushing Nasser to act.
  • UNEF Expelled: Nasser ordered UN Emergency Force peacekeepers to leave the Sinai border and deployed 100,000 Egyptian soldiers.
  • Straits of Tiran Closed (22 May): Nasser shut the Straits to Israeli ships, cutting off Israel's oil supply; Israel saw this as an act of war.
⚡ Why It Matters: Closing the Straits of Tiran cut off Israel's oil supply, giving Israel the reason to strike first.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Water Wars & Border Raids
Disputes over River Jordan water and Fatah raids led to violent clashes between Israel and Syria.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Dogfight Over Damascus
On 7 April 1967, Israeli jets shot down six Syrian fighter planes, embarrassing the Syrian government.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Nasser Mobilises Troops
Nasser kicked out UN peacekeepers and moved 100,000 soldiers to the Sinai border with Israel.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Blockade of Tiran
Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran, cutting off Israel's oil supply and triggering the Six-Day War.

Lesson 6: The Six-Day War: Pre-emptive Strike & Victory (June 1967)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 6 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Operation Focus surprise air strike (5 June 1967) • The three fronts: Sinai, West Bank/Jerusalem, and Golan Heights • Reasons for swift Israeli victory.
1. Operation Focus: The Air Blitz
Three Hours to Air Supremacy
  • Surprise Dawn Strike (5 June): At 7:45 AM, 200 Israeli jets flew low over the Mediterranean beneath Egyptian radar.
  • 300+ Planes Destroyed: Israeli bombs destroyed Egyptian runways and wiped out over 300 planes on the tarmac in 3 hours.
  • Air Supremacy: With Egypt's air force gone, Israeli jets bombed Syrian and Jordanian air bases, leaving their armies unprotected.
⚡ Why It Matters: Wiping out Egypt's air force in three hours gave Israel complete control of the skies on all fronts.
2. The Three Ground Fronts
Sinai, West Bank & Golan Heights
  • Sinai & Gaza (5–8 June): Israeli tanks smashed through Egyptian lines; Egyptian troops retreated in panic towards the Suez Canal.
  • Jerusalem & West Bank (5–7 June): Jordan opened fire; Israeli paratroopers captured the Old City of Jerusalem and the Western Wall.
  • Golan Heights (9–10 June): Israeli forces stormed steep Syrian fortified cliffs, capturing the heights and ending shelling of farms.
⚡ Why It Matters: Capturing East Jerusalem reunited the city under Israeli control and secured holy Jewish sites.
3. Why Did Israel Win So Fast?
Air Power, Training & Arab Disunity
  • Total Air Superiority: Ground armies could not fight back against constant Israeli air strikes and close air support.
  • Superb Training: Israeli commanders used flexible battlefield tactics, while Arab commanders gave rigid, confused orders.
  • Arab Division: Egypt, Jordan, and Syria did not coordinate their plans, and Egypt broadcast false claims of victory early on.
⚡ Why It Matters: Taking the Golan Heights stopped Syrian artillery shelling Israeli farms in the Galilee valley below.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Operation Focus Air Strike
Israel launched a surprise dawn air strike, destroying Egypt's air force on the ground in 3 hours.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Defeat of Egypt in Sinai
Israeli tanks swept across the Sinai Desert, defeating the Egyptian army and reaching the Suez Canal.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Capture of Jerusalem & West Bank
Israeli paratroopers captured East Jerusalem and the Western Wall, taking the entire West Bank from Jordan.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Golan Taken & Ceasefire
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria; the war ended on 10 June with Israel's territory tripled.

Lesson 7: Aftermath of 1967: The Occupied Territories & UN Res 242

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 7 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Territorial results: Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, Golan Heights, East Jerusalem • 1 million Palestinians under military rule • Khartoum Conference "Three Noes" • UN Resolution 242.
1. The Occupied Territories
Sinai, Gaza, West Bank & Golan
  • Territory Tripled: Israel gained strategic buffer zones: Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, West Bank from Jordan, and Golan from Syria.
  • 1 Million Under Military Rule: Over 1,000,000 Palestinian Arabs were suddenly placed under Israeli military administration.
  • Second Refugee Crisis: 300,000 Palestinians were displaced during the war, fleeing into Jordan and filling new refugee camps.
⚡ Why It Matters: Controlling the occupied territories gave Israel security buffers, but left 1 million Palestinians stateless.
2. The Khartoum "Three Noes"
Arab States Refuse to Yield (Aug 1967)
  • Arab Summit at Khartoum: Humiliated Arab leaders met in Sudan in August 1967 to agree their common strategy.
  • The Three Noes: They agreed: No peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, and no negotiations with Israel.
  • Impact: This hardline stance convinced Israeli leaders that they must hold on to the occupied lands for security.
⚡ Why It Matters: The "Three Noes" at Khartoum blocked all direct peace talks between Arab states and Israel.
3. UN Resolution 242 & Settlements
"Land for Peace" Formula
  • "Land for Peace" (Nov 1967): UN Res 242 stated Israel should return occupied land in exchange for Arab recognition and secure borders.
  • Ambiguous Wording: The English text said withdrawal from "territories occupied" (not all territories), causing decades of disputes.
  • First Jewish Settlements: Israel began building civilian settlements in the West Bank and Golan Heights to secure its control.
⚡ Why It Matters: UN Resolution 242 became the basis of all future peace plans: give up occupied land in return for peace.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Capture of New Lands
Israel captured Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, Golan, and Jerusalem, putting 1 million Palestinians under military rule.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Khartoum "Three Noes"
Arab leaders met at Khartoum and issued the "Three Noes": no peace, no recognition, no negotiation.
3. KEY EVENT Action: UN Resolution 242
The UN passed Resolution 242 ("Land for Peace"), but ambiguous wording caused disagreement.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Israeli Settlements
Israel began building settlements in the occupied territories, deepening Palestinian anger and making peace harder.

Lesson 8: The Rise of Palestinian Resistance: The PLO & Munich (1968–1972)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 8 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Rise of Palestinian resistance • Yasser Arafat and the PLO • Battle of Karameh (1968) • PFLP plane hijackings & Dawson's Field (1970) • Black September • Munich Olympics (1972).
1. The Rise of Yasser Arafat & The PLO
The Battle of Karameh (1968)
  • Taking Control: Palestinians lost faith in Arab rulers after 1967; they turned to guerrilla fighters called fedayeen.
  • Battle of Karameh (March 1968): Palestinian fighters resisted an Israeli raid in Jordan; though Israel won, it made Arafat a legend.
  • Arafat Leads PLO (1969): Yasser Arafat became chairman of the PLO, making it independent of Arab governments.
⚡ Why It Matters: Karameh proved Palestinians could fight for themselves, making Yasser Arafat the leader of the movement.
2. Dawson's Field & Black September (1970)
Hijackings & Expulsion from Jordan
  • Dawson's Field Hijackings (Sept 1970): The militant PFLP hijacked four airliners, flew three to Jordan, and blew them up on TV.
  • King Hussein's Crackdown: King Hussein felt his royal rule was threatened; Jordan's army attacked PLO camps in September 1970.
  • Expulsion to Lebanon: Up to 3,000 Palestinians died; the PLO was thrown out of Jordan and set up new bases in southern Lebanon.
⚡ Why It Matters: Hijackings and violence caused King Hussein to expel the PLO from Jordan into southern Lebanon.
3. The 1972 Munich Olympics Massacre
Terrorism on Live Global TV
  • Munich Massacre (Sept 1972): A terror group called "Black September" took 11 Israeli athletes hostage at the Munich Games.
  • 11 Athletes Murdered: A botched rescue by German police at the airport ended in tragedy; all 11 Israeli hostages were killed.
  • Operation Wrath of God: Israeli PM Golda Meir ordered the Mossad secret service to track down and assassinate those responsible.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Munich Olympics massacre shocked the world and led Israel to launch assassination squads against killers.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome

2. ESCALATION Escalation: Dawson's Field Skyjackings
PFLP hijacked four Western airliners to Jordan in Sept 1970, embarrassing King Hussein.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Black September in Jordan
Jordan's army attacked PLO camps in "Black September", expelling fighters into southern Lebanon.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Munich Olympics Massacre
In Sept 1972, Black September terrorists killed 11 Israeli athletes at the Munich Olympics, provoking Mossad reprisals.

Lesson 9: The War of Attrition & The Yom Kippur War (1969–1973)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 9 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: The War of Attrition (1969–70) • Causes of the 1973 Yom Kippur War • Operation Badr and Bar-Lev Line breach • Superpower airlifts • The OPEC oil embargo.
1. Sadat's Plan & Surprise Attack
6 October 1973: Holy Day Assault
  • Sadat's Goal: Sadat did not want to destroy Israel; he wanted to win back Sinai and force the USA to broker peace talks.
  • Surprise on Yom Kippur: Israel was caught completely unprepared; soldiers were praying and radio communications were quiet.
  • Operation Badr: 80,000 Egyptian troops crossed the Suez Canal and used high-pressure water hoses to blast through sand walls.
⚡ Why It Matters: President Sadat attacked to shatter the stalemate and force the USA to negotiate the return of Sinai.
2. Superpower Airlifts & Counter-Attack
US Weapons & Sharon's Crossing
  • Syrian Tank Assault: Syria attacked the Golan Heights with 1,400 tanks, nearly breaking through into northern Israel.
  • Massive US Airlift: The USA flew in emergency supplies of tanks, missiles, and ammunition (Operation Nickel Grass) to save Israel.
  • Sharon's Counter-Crossing: General Ariel Sharon led Israeli tanks across the canal, encircling Egypt's Third Army in Sinai.
⚡ Why It Matters: Crossing the canal and breaking the Bar-Lev Line restored Arab pride after the humiliation of 1967.
3. The OPEC Oil Weapon & Ceasefire
Prices Quadrupled & DEFCON 3
  • The Oil Embargo: Arab oil producers (OPEC) cut oil production and banned sales to the USA, quadrupling oil prices worldwide.
  • Nuclear Alert (DEFCON 3): When the USSR threatened to send troops to save Egypt, the USA put its nuclear forces on alert.
  • Ceasefire (25 Oct): The UN arranged a ceasefire; Israel kept territory but its sense of invincibility was permanently shattered.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Arab oil embargo proved oil could be used as a political weapon against Western economies.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Surprise Attack on Yom Kippur

2. ESCALATION Escalation: Crossing the Suez Canal
Egyptian soldiers crossed the Suez Canal and breached the Bar-Lev Line with high-pressure water hoses.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Superpower Arms Airlifts
A massive US arms airlift helped Israel counter-attack; General Sharon led tanks across the canal.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: The Arab Oil Embargo
Arab states cut oil sales to the West, quadrupling prices; a ceasefire ended fighting on 25 October.

Lesson 10: Peace with Egypt: Shuttle Diplomacy to Camp David (1974–1979)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 10 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Kissinger and shuttle diplomacy (1974–75) • Reopening of the Suez Canal (1975) • Sadat's visit to Jerusalem (1977) • Camp David Accords (1978) • Treaty of Washington (1979).
1. Kissinger's Shuttle Diplomacy
Separating the Armies (1974–75)
  • Flying Between Capitals: Because Arab states refused to talk directly to Israel, Kissinger flew between Cairo and Jerusalem over 30 times.
  • Sinai Agreements (1974–75): Egypt and Israel pulled their troops back, created UN buffer zones, and reopened the Suez Canal in June 1975.
  • Oil Embargo Ended: Kissinger's diplomacy persuaded Arab oil producers to end their oil embargo against the USA in March 1974.
⚡ Why It Matters: Sadat's visit to Jerusalem broke 30 years of Arab boycott and proved Egypt genuinely wanted peace.
2. Sadat in Jerusalem & Camp David
The 1977 Visit & 1978 Summit
  • Sadat's 1977 Gamble: Sadat shocked the world by flying to Israel and speaking to the Knesset, breaking 30 years of Arab boycott.
  • 13 Days at Camp David (1978): US President Carter isolated Sadat and Begin at his country retreat, saving talks when they nearly collapsed.
  • The Compromise: Israel agreed to withdraw from all of Sinai and dismantle its settlements in exchange for full peace and recognition.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Treaty of Washington returned all of Sinai to Egypt; Egypt was the first Arab nation to recognise Israel.
3. Treaty of Washington & The Backlash
26 March 1979 & Sadat Assassinated
  • Treaty of Washington (1979): Egypt became the first Arab country to make peace with Israel; the USA gave billions in aid to both sides.
  • Arab Outrage: Other Arab states saw Sadat as a traitor; Egypt was expelled from the Arab League and boycotted.
  • Sadat Assassinated (6 Oct 1981): Islamic extremists shot Sadat dead at a Cairo military parade because he had made peace with Israel.
⚡ Why It Matters: Arab nations boycotted Egypt, and Islamic extremists assassinated Sadat for signing the peace treaty.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Shuttle Diplomacy (1974–75)
Henry Kissinger flew between capitals to separate the armies and reopen the Suez Canal.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Sadat Visits Jerusalem
In Nov 1977, Sadat flew to Jerusalem and addressed the Israeli parliament, offering total peace.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Camp David Accords (1978)
President Carter held 13 days of talks at Camp David; Israel agreed to return Sinai in exchange for peace.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Peace Treaty & Assassination
Egypt and Israel signed the 1979 Treaty of Washington; Sadat was assassinated by extremists in 1981.

Lesson 11: The Palestinian Issue: Lebanon & The First Intifada (1974–1993)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 11 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon (Operation Peace for Galilee) • Siege of Beirut & evacuation of PLO • Sabra and Shatila massacres • The First Intifada (1987–93) and "iron fist" policy.
1. The 1982 Invasion of Lebanon
Operation Peace for Galilee
  • The Threat: The PLO controlled southern Lebanon ("Fatahland") and fired Katyusha rockets at northern Israeli towns.
  • The Invasion (June 1982): Defence Minister Ariel Sharon led Israeli forces all the way to Beirut, bombarding the city for weeks.
  • PLO Evacuated: After heavy fighting, 14,000 PLO fighters and Yasser Arafat were evacuated by sea to Tunisia.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Lebanon War expelled the PLO to Tunisia, but led to the rise of more militant groups like Hezbollah.
2. Sabra & Shatila Massacre
Phalangist Militias & Sharon Resigns
  • The Massacre (Sept 1982): Lebanese Christian fighters (Phalangists) entered the camps and murdered up to 3,500 unarmed refugees.
  • Israeli Role: Israeli soldiers had surrounded the camps and fired illumination flares at night, allowing the killings to continue.
  • Kahan Commission: An Israeli inquiry found Ariel Sharon "personally responsible" for failing to prevent it; he was forced to resign.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Sabra and Shatila massacres forced Defence Minister Ariel Sharon to resign and damaged Israel's image.
3. The First Intifada (1987–1993)
Stone-Throwers & The Iron Fist
  • The Spark (Dec 1987): An Israeli army truck crashed into cars in Gaza, killing 4 Palestinian workers; mass protests erupted.
  • Grassroots Uprising: Young Palestinians threw stones, called strikes, and refused to pay taxes against Israeli military occupation.
  • "Iron Fist" Policy: Defence Minister Rabin ordered soldiers to "break the bones" of protesters; TV images shocked the world.
⚡ Why It Matters: The First Intifada proved Palestinians in the occupied lands would resist, forcing Israel to consider talks.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Lebanon Invasion (1982)
Israel invaded Lebanon in June 1982 to crush the PLO, besieging Beirut and forcing Arafat to flee to Tunisia.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Sabra & Shatila
Christian militias massacred refugees at Sabra and Shatila, provoking worldwide outrage and Sharon's resignation.
3. KEY EVENT Action: First Intifada Erupts (1987)
In Dec 1987, Palestinian youths launched the First Intifada, throwing stones and staging strikes against Israeli rule.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Global Sympathy for Palestinians
Israel's harsh "iron fist" response was shown on TV, creating global sympathy and pressure for peace talks.

Operation Peace for Galilee The codename for the Israeli invasion of southern Lebanon in June 1982 to drive back the PLO.
Sabra & Shatila Two Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut where hundreds of civilians were murdered by Christian militias in 1982.
First Intifada The Arabic word for "shaking off"; the mass Palestinian uprising of strikes and stone-throwing from 1987 to 1993.
Iron Fist Policy The harsh military tactics used by Israeli soldiers, including tear gas, arrests, and beatings, to stop the Intifada.
📜 KEY HISTORICAL EVIDENCE: Official Israeli Judicial Inquiry Report into Sabra and Shatila
"The Minister of Defence bears personal responsibility... He did not take appropriate measures to prevent or reduce the danger of a massacre."
💡 What This Shows: Proves an official Israeli court found its own Defence Minister responsible for negligence, causing Sharon to resign.
👥 Key People
Yasser Arafat PLO Chairman who was besieged in Beirut in 1982 and forced to move his headquarters to Tunis in North Africa.
Ariel Sharon Israeli Defence Minister who directed the 1982 invasion of Lebanon and was forced to resign after the Sabra and Shatila massacres.
Yitzhak Rabin Israeli Defence Minister during the First Intifada who enforced the harsh "iron fist" policy to crush Palestinian protests.
Menachem Begin Prime Minister of Israel who approved the 1982 invasion of Lebanon, but resigned in depression in 1983 as Israeli casualties mounted.

Key Topic 3: Attempts at a solution, 1974–95

Lesson 12: Attempts at a Solution: From Oslo Accords to Oslo II (1988–1995)

Specification Cheat Sheet
Lesson 12 Revision
📋 OFFICIAL SPECIFICATION FOCUS: Arafat renounces terrorism (1988) • Madrid Conference (1991) • Secret Oslo talks • Oslo I Accord (1993) & White House handshake • Oslo II (1995) • Assassination of Yitzhak Rabin.
1. The Breakthrough to Oslo (1988–93)
Arafat Renounces Terror & Secret Talks
  • Arafat Accepts Israel (1988): Arafat spoke at the UN, rejected terrorism, and accepted UN Resolution 242 (a two-state solution).
  • Secret Oslo Talks (1993): Israeli and Palestinian envoys held secret meetings in Norway away from the media to negotiate peace.
  • Mutual Recognition: The PLO formally recognised Israel's right to exist; Israel recognised the PLO as representing Palestinians.
⚡ Why It Matters: The Oslo Accords created mutual recognition and established the Palestinian Authority in Gaza and Jericho.
2. The Oslo I Accords (1993)
The White House Lawn Handshake
  • Historic Handshake (13 Sept 1993): PM Rabin and Chairman Arafat shook hands in front of US President Bill Clinton.
  • Palestinian Authority (PNA): Set up an elected Palestinian government with self-rule over the Gaza Strip and town of Jericho.
  • Five-Year Transition: Difficult issues (Jerusalem, refugees, borders, and Jewish settlements) were postponed for 5 years.
⚡ Why It Matters: Oslo II divided the West Bank into separate zones, leaving Israel in military control of over 70% of the land.
3. Oslo II & Rabin's Assassination
Areas A, B, C & 4 November 1995
  • Oslo II (1995): Divided West Bank: Area A (Palestinian control), Area B (shared control), Area C (Israeli military control).
  • Extremist Violence: Militant Islamic group Hamas launched suicide bus bombings inside Israel to destroy the peace process.
  • Rabin Assassinated (4 Nov 1995): Jewish extremist Yigal Amir shot Yitzhak Rabin dead at a Tel Aviv peace rally, wrecking the peace process.
⚡ Why It Matters: Rabin's assassination by a Jewish extremist and Hamas suicide bus bombings severely derailed the peace process.
🔗 Step-by-Step: What Happened & Why (Narrative Account • Q2 Guide) 1. Trigger ➔ 2. Escalation ➔ 3. Key Event ➔ 4. Outcome
1. TRIGGER Trigger: Arafat Renounces Terror
In 1988, Arafat renounced terrorism; secret talks in Norway in 1993 opened the path to peace.
2. ESCALATION Escalation: Oslo I Handshake (1993)
Rabin and Arafat signed the Oslo Accords in Sept 1993, creating the Palestinian Authority in Gaza and Jericho.
3. KEY EVENT Action: Oslo II Division (1995)
In 1995, Oslo II divided the West Bank into Areas A, B, and C; Jordan signed peace with Israel.
4. OUTCOME Outcome: Rabin Assassinated (1995)
On 4 Nov 1995, Israeli PM Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead by a Jewish extremist, shattering hopes for lasting peace.

Oslo Accords The 1993 peace agreements establishing mutual recognition and Palestinian self-government.
Palestinian Authority (PNA) The official self-governing Palestinian body set up in 1994 to administer parts of Gaza and the West Bank.
Oslo II (Areas A, B, C) The 1995 agreement dividing the West Bank into Palestinian-controlled (A), shared (B), and Israeli-controlled (C) areas.
Two-State Solution The proposal for an independent State of Palestine existing peacefully alongside the State of Israel.
📜 KEY HISTORICAL EVIDENCE: Official Address Following the Signing of the Oslo Accords
"We, the soldiers who have returned from the battle stained with blood... say to you today in a loud and clear voice: Enough of blood and tears. Enough."
💡 What This Shows: Shows a former Israeli general committing to peace with Palestinians, leading to the creation of the Palestinian Authority.
👥 Key People
Yitzhak Rabin Israeli Prime Minister who signed the Oslo Accords and shook hands with Arafat; murdered by a Jewish extremist in Nov 1995.
Yasser Arafat PLO Chairman who renounced terrorism in 1988, signed the Oslo Accords, and became President of the Palestinian Authority.
Bill Clinton US President who hosted the historic 13 September 1993 signing ceremony of the Oslo Accords on the White House lawn.
King Hussein of Jordan King of Jordan who signed a historic peace treaty with Israel in October 1994, becoming the second Arab nation to make peace.

Cartographic Atlas 2 • The June 1967 Blitzkrieg

The 1967 Six-Day War & The Occupied Territories

Map Atlas 2
1. Operation Focus: The Dawn Air Strike
• Surprise Strike (5 June): At 7:45 AM, 200 Israeli jets flew low under Egyptian radar over the Mediterranean Sea.
• 300+ Planes Destroyed: In 3 hours, Israel wiped out the Egyptian air force on the ground, winning complete control of the skies.
• Decisive Advantage: Without air protection, ground armies from Egypt, Jordan, and Syria could not defend themselves.
2. Fighting on Three Fronts
• Sinai Front: Israeli tanks smashed through Egyptian lines, reaching the Suez Canal in four days and capturing all of Sinai.
• Jerusalem & West Bank: Israeli paratroopers captured East Jerusalem and the Western Wall on 7 June, taking the West Bank from Jordan.
• Golan Heights: On 9–10 June, Israeli forces stormed Syrian bunker positions on the high cliffs of the Golan Heights.
3. The Occupied Territories
• Territory Tripled: Israel captured 70,000 sq km: the Sinai Desert, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights.
• 1 Million Palestinians: Israel was now in military control of over 1 million Palestinian Arabs living in the West Bank and Gaza.
• Strategic Buffers: Israel gained natural barriers (Suez Canal, River Jordan, Golan Heights) to protect its heartland.
4. Diplomatic Results
• Khartoum "Three Noes": Arab leaders refused to make peace, recognize Israel, or negotiate with Israel.
• UN Resolution 242: Called for "Land for Peace" (Israel returns occupied land in return for Arab recognition and security).
• Rise of the PLO: Humiliated Arab armies lost credibility; Palestinians turned to Yasser Arafat's PLO to fight for themselves.

Cartographic Atlas 2 • The Oslo Peace Process (1993–1995)

The 1995 Oslo II Division: Areas A, B, and C

Map Atlas 2
1. Area A: Full Palestinian Control (~3%)
• Towns & Cities: Included 8 major Palestinian cities: Ramallah, Nablus, Jenin, Bethlehem, Jericho, Qalqilya, Tulkarm, and parts of Hebron.
• Palestinian Authority: The PNA had full control over civil affairs (schools, police, hospitals).
• Islands of Control: Area A formed separate, disconnected islands surrounded by Israeli-controlled roads.
2. Area B: Shared Control (~25%)
• Villages: Included approximately 450 Palestinian villages across the West Bank.
• Shared Responsibility: The Palestinian Authority handled civil matters, but the Israeli military maintained security control.
• Checkpoints: Israeli soldiers could enter Area B at any time to arrest suspects, and set up military checkpoints.
3. Area C: Full Israeli Control (~72%)
• Majority of Land: Israel kept total civil and military control over nearly three-quarters of the West Bank.
• Jewish Settlements: Encompassed all 130+ Jewish settlements, major roads, water resources, and the Jordan Valley border.
• Settler Population: Increased rapidly from 110,000 to over 200,000 during the 1990s peace talks, creating deep anger.
4. Why the Peace Process Failed
• Difficult Issues Postponed: Oslo delayed the hardest problems: the status of Jerusalem, refugee return, and final borders.
• Extremist Violence: Militant Islamic group Hamas launched suicide bus bombings inside Israel to destroy the peace process.
• Rabin Assassinated: On 4 November 1995, Israeli PM Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead by a Jewish extremist opposed to Oslo.

Paper 2 Master Revision • Summary & Exam Strategy

Conflict in the Middle East: Master Revision & Exam Checklist

Final Summary
The Six Key Turning Points of the Conflict (1945–1995) Must-Know Historical Milestones
1. 1948–49 War & Al-Nakba Israel declared independence; five Arab armies invaded. Israel won and expanded to 79% of land. Over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs became refugees in UNRWA camps.
2. 1956 Suez Crisis Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal. Britain, France, and Israel secretly attacked Egypt. US President Eisenhower forced them to withdraw, ending British imperial power.
3. 1967 Six-Day War Israel destroyed Egypt's air force in a surprise strike and captured Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, Golan, and East Jerusalem. UN passed Resolution 242 ('Land for Peace').
4. 1973 Yom Kippur War Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Yom Kippur, crossing the Suez Canal. Arab oil states launched an oil embargo, quadrupling prices and forcing peace talks.
5. 1979 Treaty of Washington Sadat visited Jerusalem in 1977. Carter hosted Camp David (1978). Egypt became the first Arab state to recognise Israel, reclaiming Sinai; Sadat was assassinated in 1981.
6. 1993 Oslo I Accords After the 1987 Intifada, secret talks led to the White House handshake between Rabin and Arafat. The Palestinian Authority was set up, but Rabin was murdered in 1995.
12 Key Words You Must Know for the Exam Quick Glossary
• Mandate: British control over Palestine (1920–48).
• Zionism: Movement for a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
• Al-Nakba: Arabic for 'Catastrophe' (1948 refugees).
• Green Line: The 1949 armistice borders of Israel.
• Nationalisation: Government takeover of the Suez Canal.
• UNEF: UN Emergency Force peacekeepers in Sinai.
• UN Res 242: 1967 'Land for Peace' formula.
• Fedayeen: Armed Palestinian guerrilla fighters.
• Bar-Lev Line: Israeli sand-wall forts along Suez.
• Shuttle Diplomacy: Kissinger flying between capitals.
• First Intifada: 1987–93 Palestinian stone-throwing uprising.
• Oslo Accords: 1993–95 peace deals creating Palestinian rule.
